amc12-ahsme-1962-01.title: Simplify numerator and denominator
amc12-ahsme-1962-01.body:
Any power of $1$ is $1$, so the numerator is $1$. The denominator is $\frac15+\frac13=\frac{3+5}{15}=\frac{8}{15}$.

So the expression is $\dfrac{1}{8/15}=\dfrac{15}{8}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{15}{8}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-02.title: Common denominator first
amc12-ahsme-1962-02.body:
$\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{4-3}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}$. It is positive, which rules out (B) and (C) immediately.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-03.title: Middle term is the average
amc12-ahsme-1962-03.body:
In an arithmetic progression the middle term is the average of its neighbours: $2(x+1)=(x-1)+(2x+3)$, i.e. $2x+2=3x+2$, so $x=0$.

Check: the terms are $-1, 1, 3$, with common difference $2$.

**Answer: (B) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-03.title: Equal differences
amc12-ahsme-1962-03.body:
The differences must be equal: $(x+1)-(x-1)=2$ and $(2x+3)-(x+1)=x+2$. So $x+2=2$, giving $x=0$.

**Answer: (B) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-05.title: Definition of π
amc12-ahsme-1962-05.body:
For **every** circle, circumference $\div$ diameter $=\pi$. With new radius $r+1$: $\dfrac{2\pi(r+1)}{2(r+1)}=\pi$.

**Answer: (C) $\pi$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-06.title: Find the side of the triangle
amc12-ahsme-1962-06.body:
An equilateral triangle with side $s$ has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$. So $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2=9\sqrt3$, $s^2=36$, $s=6$.

The perimeter is $18$, so the square has side $\frac{18}{4}=\frac92$ and diagonal $\frac92\sqrt2=\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-07.title: Angle sum in triangle BDC
amc12-ahsme-1962-07.body:
The exterior angle at $B$ is $180-B$, so $\angle DBC=\frac12(180-B)=90-\frac B2$. Similarly $\angle DCB=90-\frac C2$.

Then $\angle BDC=180-\left(90-\frac B2\right)-\left(90-\frac C2\right)=\frac{B+C}{2}=\frac{180-A}{2}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac12(180-A)$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-07.title: Test a special triangle
amc12-ahsme-1962-07.body:
Take a right isosceles triangle: $A=90$, $B=C=45$. The exterior angles at $B$ and $C$ are $135$, so $\angle DBC=\angle DCB=67.5$ and $\angle BDC=45$.

The choices give (A) $0$, (B) $0$, (C) $45$, (D) $90$, (E) $0$ — only (C) fits.

**Answer: (C) $\frac12(180-A)$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-08.title: Add and divide
amc12-ahsme-1962-08.body:
The sum is $(n-1)\cdot 1+\left(1-\frac1n\right)=n-\frac1n$. Dividing by $n$: mean $=1-\frac{1}{n^2}$.

**Answer: (D) $1-\frac{1}{n^2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-08.title: Shortfall view
amc12-ahsme-1962-08.body:
If all numbers were $1$, the mean would be $1$. One number is short by $\frac1n$, which lowers the mean by $\frac{1/n}{n}=\frac1{n^2}$.

**Answer: (D) $1-\frac{1}{n^2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-09.title: Repeated difference of squares
amc12-ahsme-1962-09.body:
$x^9-x=x(x^8-1)=x(x^4+1)(x^4-1)=x(x^4+1)(x^2+1)(x+1)(x-1)$.

$x^4+1$ and $x^2+1$ cannot be factored further over the integers (no real roots for $x^2+1$; $x^4+1$ has no rational roots and no factorization $(x^2+ax+b)(x^2+cx+d)$ with integers). That's $5$ factors.

**Answer: (B) $5$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-10.title: Compute both rates
amc12-ahsme-1962-10.body:
Going: $150\div 3\frac13=150\cdot\frac{3}{10}=45$ mph.

Whole trip: $300$ miles in $3\frac13+4\frac16=7\frac12$ hours, so $r=300\div 7.5=40$ mph.

$45-40=5$.

**Answer: (A) $5$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-11.title: Quadratic formula
amc12-ahsme-1962-11.body:
The difference of the roots of $x^2+bx+c$ is $\sqrt{b^2-4c}=\sqrt{p^2-(p^2-1)}=1$.

**Answer: (B) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-11.title: Factor
amc12-ahsme-1962-11.body:
Multiply by 4: $4x^2-4px+p^2-1=(2x-p)^2-1=(2x-p-1)(2x-p+1)$. Roots $\frac{p+1}{2}$ and $\frac{p-1}{2}$ differ by $1$.

**Answer: (B) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-12.title: Binomial theorem
amc12-ahsme-1962-12.body:
$\left(1-\frac1a\right)^6=\sum_{k=0}^{6}\binom6k(-1)^k a^{-k}$. The last three terms are $k=4,5,6$ with coefficients $\binom64=15$, $-\binom65=-6$, $\binom66=1$. Sum: $15-6+1=10$.

**Answer: (C) $10$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-12.title: Rewrite as a polynomial
amc12-ahsme-1962-12.body:
$\left(1-\frac1a\right)^6=\frac{(a-1)^6}{a^6}$. The last three coefficients are those of $a^2,a^1,a^0$ in $(a-1)^6$: $15, -6, 1$, summing to $10$.

**Answer: (C) $10$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-15.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1962-15.body:
The centroid is $G=\frac{A+B+C}{3}$. If $C=P+t\vec v$ runs along a line, then $G=\frac{A+B+P}{3}+\frac t3\vec v$ also runs along a line (parallel to the first).

**Answer: (D) a straight line**

amc12-ahsme-1962-15.title: Homothety
amc12-ahsme-1962-15.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ (fixed). The centroid lies on $MC$ with $MG=\frac13 MC$, so $G$ is the image of $C$ under the dilation with centre $M$ and factor $\frac13$. A dilation maps lines to lines.

**Answer: (D) a straight line**

amc12-ahsme-1962-16.title: Sides of R₂
amc12-ahsme-1962-16.body:
$R_1$ is $2\times 6$, so its sides are in ratio $1:3$. Let $R_2$ be $x\times 3x$; its diagonal is $x\sqrt{10}=15$, so $x^2=\frac{225}{10}$. Area $=3x^2=\frac{675}{10}=\frac{135}{2}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{135}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-16.title: Scale factor squared
amc12-ahsme-1962-16.body:
$R_1$ has diagonal $\sqrt{4+36}=\sqrt{40}$. Areas scale by the square of the ratio of diagonals: $12\cdot\frac{225}{40}=\frac{135}{2}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{135}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-18.title: Twelve triangles
amc12-ahsme-1962-18.body:
Join the centre to the vertices: $12$ isosceles triangles with two sides $r$ and apex angle $30^\circ$. Each has area $\frac12 r^2\sin30^\circ=\frac{r^2}{4}$. Total: $12\cdot\frac{r^2}{4}=3r^2$.

**Answer: (A) $3r^2$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-18.title: Without trigonometry
amc12-ahsme-1962-18.body:
Take one triangle $OAB$ with $\angle AOB=30^\circ$. Drop the perpendicular from $B$ to $OA$: in the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle it has length $\frac r2$. So the area is $\frac12\cdot r\cdot\frac r2=\frac{r^2}{4}$, and $12$ of them give $3r^2$.

**Answer: (A) $3r^2$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-19.title: a+b+c is y(1)
amc12-ahsme-1962-19.body:
$a+b+c$ is the value at $x=1$. Using $y=5+bx+ax^2$ with the solved $a=1,b=-6$: $y=x^2-6x+5=(x-1)(x-5)$, which vanishes at $x=1$.

**Answer: (C) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-20.title: Middle term
amc12-ahsme-1962-20.body:
The angles of a pentagon sum to $540^\circ$. Write them as $m-2d, m-d, m, m+d, m+2d$; their sum is $5m=540$, so the middle angle is $m=108^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $108$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-21.title: Conjugate roots
amc12-ahsme-1962-21.body:
Real coefficients force the other root to be $3-2i$. Product of roots: $\frac s2=(3+2i)(3-2i)=9+4=13$, so $s=26$.

**Answer: (E) $26$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-21.title: Build the quadratic
amc12-ahsme-1962-21.body:
The monic quadratic with roots $3\pm2i$ is $(x-3)^2+4=x^2-6x+13$. Multiplying by $2$: $2x^2-12x+26$, so $s=26$ (and $r=-12$).

**Answer: (E) $26$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-22.title: Expand
amc12-ahsme-1962-22.body:
$121_b=b^2+2b+1=(b+1)^2$, always a perfect square. The only restriction is that the digit $2$ must be allowed, i.e. $b>2$.

**Answer: (D) $b>2$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-23.title: Two expressions for the area
amc12-ahsme-1962-23.body:
Twice the area is $AB\cdot CD=BC\cdot AE$, so $BC=\dfrac{AB\cdot CD}{AE}$ is known. Then in right triangle $CDB$: $DB=\sqrt{BC^2-CD^2}$, which is known whatever the angles are.

So $DB$ is always determined; none of (A)–(D) is correct.

**Answer: (E) none of these is correct**

amc12-ahsme-1962-23.title: Similar triangles
amc12-ahsme-1962-23.body:
Triangles $BDC$ and $BEA$ are right triangles sharing angle $B$ (or its supplement if $B$ is obtuse — the acute angle at $B$ is the same either way), so they are similar: $\frac{CD}{AE}=\frac{BC}{AB}$. That gives $BC$, and then $DB$ by Pythagoras, in every case.

**Answer: (E) none of these is correct**

amc12-ahsme-1962-24.title: Add the rates
amc12-ahsme-1962-24.body:
Rates: $\frac1{x+6}+\frac1{x+1}+\frac1{2x}=\frac1x$, so $\frac1{x+6}+\frac1{x+1}=\frac1{2x}$.

Clearing denominators: $2x(x+1)+2x(x+6)=(x+6)(x+1)$, i.e. $4x^2+14x=x^2+7x+6$, so $3x^2+7x-6=0=(3x-2)(x+3)$. Since $x>0$, $x=\frac23$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac23$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-24.title: Check the choices
amc12-ahsme-1962-24.body:
For $x=\frac23$: P takes $\frac{20}{3}$ h, Q $\frac53$ h, R $\frac43$ h. Combined rate $\frac3{20}+\frac35+\frac34=\frac{3+12+15}{20}=\frac32$ jobs per hour, i.e. $\frac23$ h per job. ✓

**Answer: (A) $\frac23$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-25.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1962-25.body:
Put $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,8)$, and side $BC$ on the line $x=8$. The centre is on the perpendicular bisector of $AD$: $(h,4)$. Tangency to $x=8$ gives $r=8-h$, and $r^2=h^2+16$.

So $(8-h)^2=h^2+16$, $64-16h=16$, $h=3$, $r=5$.

**Answer: (C) $5$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-25.title: Right triangle
amc12-ahsme-1962-25.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AD$ and $O$ the centre; $OM\perp AD$ and the tangent point is the midpoint of $BC$, so $OM=8-r$. In right triangle $OMA$: $r^2=4^2+(8-r)^2$, which gives $16r=80$, $r=5$.

**Answer: (C) $5$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-26.title: Vertex
amc12-ahsme-1962-26.body:
The parabola opens downward with vertex at $x=\frac{8}{6}=\frac43$. Value: $8\cdot\frac43-3\cdot\frac{16}{9}=\frac{32}{3}-\frac{16}{3}=\frac{16}{3}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{16}{3}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-27.title: Check each rule
amc12-ahsme-1962-27.body:
(1) The larger of $a,b$ doesn't depend on order. ✓

(2) Both sides are the largest of $a,b,c$. ✓

(3) If $a$ is at least $\max(b,c)$, both sides equal $\max(b,c)$. Otherwise the left side is $a$ if $a$ is below $\max(b,c)$… more carefully: the left side is $\min(a,\max(b,c))$. On the right, $\max(\min(a,b),\min(a,c))$. Say $b\ge c$: then $\min(a,b)\ge\min(a,c)$, so the right side is $\min(a,b)=\min(a,\max(b,c))$. ✓

**Answer: (E) all three**

amc12-ahsme-1962-27.title: Think of numbers on a line
amc12-ahsme-1962-27.body:
Sort the three numbers. For (3): capping $b$ and $c$ at the height $a$ and then taking the bigger is the same as taking the bigger first and then capping it at $a$ — capping is an increasing operation, so it preserves which one is bigger. (1) and (2) are clear.

**Answer: (E) all three**

amc12-ahsme-1962-28.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1962-28.body:
$x=10$: $10^1=10$ and $\frac{1000}{100}=10$ ✓. $x=100$: $100^2=10^4$ and $\frac{10^6}{100}=10^4$ ✓. A quadratic in $t$ has at most two roots, so there are no others.

**Answer: (D) 10 or 100, only**

amc12-ahsme-1962-29.title: Factor
amc12-ahsme-1962-29.body:
$2x^2+x-6=(2x-3)(x+2)<0$. The upward parabola is negative between its roots: $-2<x<\frac32$.

**Answer: (A) $-2<x<\frac32$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-29.title: Test points
amc12-ahsme-1962-29.body:
$x=0$ works ($0<6$), which rules out (B), (D), (E). $x=-3$ fails ($15\not<6$), which rules out (C).

**Answer: (A) $-2<x<\frac32$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-30.title: Negation of an 'and'
amc12-ahsme-1962-30.body:
The negation of "$p$ and $q$ are both true" is "at least one of $p,q$ is false". Statements (2), (3), (4) each have a false component, so each implies it; (1) contradicts it. That's $3$.

**Answer: (D) $3$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-31.title: Diophantine equation
amc12-ahsme-1962-31.body:
An $n$-gon has interior angle $\frac{180(n-2)}{n}$. We need $\frac{(n-2)/n}{(m-2)/m}=\frac32$, i.e. $2m(n-2)=3n(m-2)$, which simplifies to $mn+4m-6n=0$, so
$$m=\frac{6n}{n+4}=6-\frac{24}{n+4}.$$
We need $m\ge3$ an integer, so $n+4$ divides $24$ and $n+4\ge 8$: $n+4\in\{8,12,24\}$, giving $(n,m)=(4,3),(8,4),(20,5)$.

**Answer: (C) $3$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-31.title: Check them
amc12-ahsme-1962-31.body:
Square $90^\circ$ vs triangle $60^\circ$; octagon $135^\circ$ vs square $90^\circ$; 20-gon $162^\circ$ vs pentagon $108^\circ$. Each ratio is $3:2$. Since $m<6$ always (angles of the larger polygon are below $180^\circ$, so the smaller is below $120^\circ$), only $m=3,4,5$ are possible, each giving one $n$.

**Answer: (C) $3$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-32.title: Test n = 1 and n = 2
amc12-ahsme-1962-32.body:
$n=1$: sum $1$. (E) gives $\frac44=1$; (D) gives $\frac12$, (A) $1$, (B) $2$, (C) $0$. $n=2$: sum $1+\frac32=\frac52$; (E) gives $\frac{10}{4}=\frac52$, (A) gives $\frac32$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{n^2+3n}{4}$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-33.title: Distance from 1
amc12-ahsme-1962-33.body:
$|x-1|$ is the distance from $x$ to $1$. Distances between $2$ and $5$: to the right $3\le x\le 6$, to the left $-4\le x\le -1$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1962-33.title: Cases
amc12-ahsme-1962-33.body:
If $x\ge1$: $2\le x-1\le5$, so $3\le x\le 6$. If $x<1$: $2\le 1-x\le 5$, so $-4\le x\le -1$.

**Answer: (A)**

amc12-ahsme-1962-34.title: Discriminant
amc12-ahsme-1962-34.body:
Rewrite: $K^2x^2-(3K^2+1)x+2K^2=0$. If $K=0$ this is $x=0$, a real root. Otherwise the discriminant is
$$(3K^2+1)^2-8K^4=K^4+6K^2+1>0.$$
So there are real roots for every real $K$.

**Answer: (E) all**

amc12-ahsme-1962-34.title: Graphical view
amc12-ahsme-1962-34.body:
For $K\ne0$, the parabola $y=K^2(x-1)(x-2)$ is negative between $1$ and $2$ and grows without bound, while $y=x$ is positive there. At $x=1$ the line is above the parabola ($1>0$), and for large $x$ the parabola is above the line, so they cross. Hence real roots always exist.

**Answer: (E) all**

amc12-ahsme-1962-35.title: Angle formula
amc12-ahsme-1962-35.body:
At $m$ minutes after 6:00 the hour hand is at $180+0.5m$ degrees and the minute hand at $6m$ degrees. The angle is $|180-5.5m|=110$, so $5.5m=70$ or $5.5m=290$, i.e. $m=\frac{140}{11}$ or $m=\frac{580}{11}$.

Time away: $\frac{440}{11}=40$ minutes.

**Answer: (B) $40$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-35.title: Relative speed
amc12-ahsme-1962-35.body:
The minute hand gains $5.5^\circ$ per minute on the hour hand. Between the two times it goes from $110^\circ$ behind to $110^\circ$ ahead, gaining $220^\circ$: $220\div5.5=40$ minutes.

**Answer: (B) $40$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-36.title: Two powers of 2 differing by 2
amc12-ahsme-1962-36.body:
The left side is an integer, so $y\ge0$. The factors $x-8$ and $x-10$ differ by $2$ and their product is a power of $2$, so both are $\pm$ powers of $2$ with the same sign. Powers of $2$ differing by $2$: only $2$ and $4$. So $(x-10,x-8)=(2,4)$ or $(-4,-2)$, giving $x=12$ or $x=6$, both with $2^y=8$, $y=3$.

That is $2$ solution pairs: $(12,3)$ and $(6,3)$.

**Answer: (C) $2$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-36.title: Substitute u = x − 9
amc12-ahsme-1962-36.body:
$(u+1)(u-1)=u^2-1=2^y$. $u^2=2^y+1$: $y=0$ gives $2$ (not square), $y=1$ gives $3$, $y=2$ gives $5$, $y=3$ gives $9$ ✓. For $y\ge 3$, $u$ is odd and $u^2-1=(u-1)(u+1)$ is a product of two consecutive even numbers, one of which is $\equiv 2\pmod 4$; for a power of 2 that factor must be $\pm2$, forcing $u=\pm3$. So $u=\pm3$ only.

**Answer: (C) $2$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-37.title: Subtract two triangles
amc12-ahsme-1962-37.body:
Let $AE=AF=x$. Removing triangles $AEF$ (area $\frac{x^2}{2}$) and $EBC$ (legs $1-x$ and $1$, area $\frac{1-x}{2}$) from the square leaves
$$[CDFE]=1-\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{1-x}{2}=\frac12+\frac x2-\frac{x^2}{2}.$$
This is maximal at $x=\frac12$: $\frac12+\frac14-\frac18=\frac58$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac58$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-39.title: Triangle of medians
amc12-ahsme-1962-39.body:
The medians of a triangle can form a triangle whose area is $\frac34$ of the original: here $\frac34\cdot3\sqrt{15}=\frac{9\sqrt{15}}{4}$.

Heron's formula in the form $16K^2=2(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2)-(a^4+b^4+c^4)$ with sides $3,6,m$:
$$16\cdot\frac{81\cdot15}{16}=1215=2(324+45m^2)-(1377+m^4),$$
so $m^4-90m^2+1944=0$, $(m^2-36)(m^2-54)=0$.

$m=6$ would make two medians equal, which happens only when two sides are equal — excluded. So $m=\sqrt{54}=3\sqrt6$.

**Answer: (C) $3\sqrt6$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-39.title: Coordinates with the centroid
amc12-ahsme-1962-39.body:
Let $G$ be the centroid and put the medians from $A$ and $B$ along vectors: $\vec{GA}=\mathbf u$, $\vec{GB}=\mathbf v$ with $|\mathbf u|=2$, $|\mathbf v|=4$ (two-thirds of $3$ and $6$), and $\vec{GC}=-\mathbf u-\mathbf v$. Area of $ABC$ is $3[GAB]=\frac32|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=12\sin\theta=3\sqrt{15}$, so $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}$, $\cos\theta=\pm\frac14$.

Third median $=\frac32|\mathbf u+\mathbf v|=\frac32\sqrt{4+16+16\cos\theta}=\frac32\sqrt{24}$ or $\frac32\sqrt{16}$, i.e. $3\sqrt6$ or $6$. As above, $6$ is excluded.

**Answer: (C) $3\sqrt6$**

amc12-ahsme-1962-40.title: Sum of geometric series
amc12-ahsme-1962-40.body:
Write $S$ as a sum of geometric tails: $S=\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{n\ge k}10^{-n}=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{10^{-k}}{1-\frac1{10}}=\frac{10}{9}\cdot\frac19=\frac{10}{81}$. (Decimal check: $0.1+0.02+0.003+\dots=0.123456\ldots\approx0.12345679=\frac{10}{81}$.)

**Answer: (B) $\frac{10}{81}$**
